summary.text: A finite check shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\) there are primes \(p,q\nmid d\) with different final decimal digits and \(pq\le150\). Since \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), some index \(0\le i<pq\) makes \(a+id\) divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\), so one of the first \(150\) terms has prime divisors with different final digits.

full_proof.text:
Call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same residue modulo \(10\). (For the progression under discussion every term is at least \(2\), so the harmless convention concerning the integer \(1\) in the OEIS sequence is irrelevant.) We prove that no arithmetic progression of the stated kind exists.

We first establish a lemma about every possible common difference.

**Lemma.** For every integer \(d\) with \(1\le d\le 2025\), there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
p\nmid d,\qquad q\nmid d,\qquad pq\le 150,
\]
and \(p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}\).

**Proof of the lemma.** Suppose, to the contrary, that for a particular \(d\le 2025\) no such pair exists. Thus, for every pair of primes in the list of pairs used below, at least one member of the pair must divide \(d\). All of these pairs have different final decimal digits and product at most \(150\).

We successively determine forced prime divisors of \(d\).

1. First, \(2\mid d\). Indeed, if \(2\nmid d\), consider the five pairs
\[
(2,3),\ (2,5),\ (2,7),\ (2,11),\ (2,13).
\]
Their products are respectively \(6,10,14,22,26\), all at most \(150\), and in each pair the two primes have different residues modulo \(10\). Since by assumption neither member of any admissible pair can simultaneously fail to divide \(d\), the supposition \(2\nmid d\) forces
\[
3\mid d,\quad 5\mid d,\quad 7\mid d,\quad 11\mid d,\quad 13\mid d.
\]
These are distinct primes, so their product divides \(d\). Hence
\[
15015=3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\mid d,
\]
which is impossible because \(1\le d\le2025\). Therefore \(2\mid d\).

2. Next, \(3\mid d\). If \(3\nmid d\), use the four pairs
\[
(3,5),\ (3,7),\ (3,11),\ (3,17).
\]
Their products are \(15,21,33,51\), and their terminal-digit pairs are respectively \((3,5),(3,7),(3,1),(3,7)\), so all are admissible. The absence of a usable pair forces
\[
5\mid d,\quad7\mid d,\quad11\mid d,\quad17\mid d.
\]
Together with the already proved divisibility \(2\mid d\), this gives
\[
13090=2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17\mid d,
\]
again contradicting \(d\le2025\). Thus \(3\mid d\).

3. We next show \(5\mid d\). If \(5\nmid d\), consider
\[
(5,7),\ (5,11),\ (5,13).
\]
Their products are \(35,55,65\), and their members have distinct final digits. Therefore \(7,11,13\) would all have to divide \(d\). Since \(2\mid d\) and \(3\mid d\) as well, the product of these five distinct primes divides \(d\):
\[
6006=2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\mid d.
\]
This contradicts the upper bound on \(d\). Consequently \(5\mid d\).

4. We also have \(7\mid d\). Otherwise the two pairs
\[
(7,11),\ (7,13)
\]
would force both \(11\mid d\) and \(13\mid d\). These pairs have products \(77\) and \(91\), and the final digit \(7\) differs from both \(1\) and \(3\). Combining the forced divisibilities with \(2\mid d\), \(3\mid d\), and \(5\mid d\), we would obtain
\[
4290=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13\mid d,
\]
which is again too large. Hence \(7\mid d\).

We have now proved
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210\mid d.
\]
Finally consider the pair \((11,13)\). Its product is \(143\le150\), and \(11\equiv1\pmod {10}\) whereas \(13\equiv3\pmod {10}\). Our assumption that no usable pair exists says that at least one of \(11,13\) divides \(d\). If \(11\mid d\), then, because all the primes involved are distinct,
\[
2310=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\mid d;
\]
if \(13\mid d\), then
\[
2730=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\mid d.
\]
Either alternative implies \(d>2025\), the final contradiction. This proves the lemma.

We now apply the lemma to a proposed progression. Suppose that integers \(a,d\) satisfy
\[
a\ge2,\qquad 1\le d\le2025.
\]
Choose primes \(p,q\) supplied by the lemma. In particular, neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Because \(p\) and \(q\) have different residues modulo \(10\), they are distinct. Since they are prime and neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Therefore \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). The congruence
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod {pq}
\]
has a solution modulo \(pq\), explicitly
\[
i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod {pq}.
\]
Choose its unique representative satisfying
\[
0\le i<pq.
\]
Since \(pq\le150\), this gives \(0\le i<150\). Thus \(a+id\) is one of the first \(150\) terms of the progression, indexed from \(i=0\) through \(i=149\).

By the defining congruence,
\[
pq\mid a+id.
\]
In particular, both primes \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\). This term is positive (indeed it is at least \(a\ge2\)). Its set of prime divisors therefore contains \(p\) and \(q\), whose final decimal digits differ. Consequently the prime divisors of \(a+id\) do not all share one final decimal digit, so \(a+id\) is not lopsided and does not satisfy the defining condition for A381159.

We have shown that for every starting value \(a\ge2\) and every positive common difference \(d\le2025\), at least one of the terms
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
fails to belong to A381159. Hence there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which all \(150\) terms occur in the sequence. This disproves the conjecture.
